system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 7 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2137-10-05 15:03:00 to 2137-10-11 16:40:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___ was admitted for a scheduled bronchoscopy with balloon dilation due to recurrent tracheobronchial stenosis from relapsing polychondritis and Ruvalcaba-Myhre-Smith syndrome. The procedure was performed without complications, and he was observed post-operatively. His breathing remained stable, and pain was controlled with oxycodone. Elevated white blood cell count persisted but was attributed to chronic inflammation rather than active infection, supported by the absence of fever or increased secretions. He was started on a prednisone taper from 50 mg to his baseline 7.5 mg and discharged home in stable condition with follow-up planned in pulmonology and rheumatology.
problems: Other specified diseases of upper respiratory tract
Other diseases of bronchus, not elsewhere classified
Elevated white blood cell count, unspecified

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during this admission. Can you tell me what’s been going on with your breathing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hey, thanks. I’ve been having more trouble breathing, especially at night. I’ve had to wear my humidifier all day and night now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Your dad mentioned your secretions have increased too. Any fever, chills, or coughing up blood?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, no fever or night sweats. Just more mucus and shortness of breath, like before my last dilation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. We checked your labs and your white blood cell count is high, which suggests inflammation or infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it an infection? I’ve had pseudomonas before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your sputum culture showed Pseudomonas aeruginosa. We’re starting IV antibiotics—cefepime—to treat it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need another dilation? I was supposed to have one soon anyway.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning a bronchoscopy in the next day or two. Given your symptoms and history, we expect to do another dilation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s what usually helps. What about my prednisone? I’m on 7.5 mg daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re increasing it to 20 mg daily to reduce airway inflammation. Then we’ll taper it down over a few weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my methotrexate? I missed a dose last week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Rheumatology said it’s okay—you’re on a weekly dose, and the medicine lasts a while. We’ll restart it as scheduled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your chest X-ray yesterday didn’t show pneumonia, but we’re still concerned about tracheal infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the antibiotics are for the trachea, not lungs?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. It’s called tracheobronchitis. The Pseudomonas is in your airways, causing swelling and more mucus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. I feel a bit better already with the humidifier and meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. We’ll proceed with bronchoscopy tomorrow to clean out secretions and dilate the narrowed areas.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, we’re getting ready for your bronchoscopy. They found a new shadow on your left lung this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it pneumonia? I thought the X-ray was clear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, there’s a small area of consolidation. But after your procedure earlier, the follow-up X-ray shows it’s already improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did well during the bronchoscopy. We dilated your trachea and left main bronchus. There was a lot of inflammation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is the blockage worse than before?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The trachea was about 70% narrowed. We opened it up. The left bronchus was completely blocked—we cleared and dilated it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds intense. Did you take any samples?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we took washings and a small biopsy. Cultures confirmed Pseudomonas, which is sensitive to your current antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your repeat X-ray looks better—no pneumonia now. Lung volumes are still low, but that’s typical for you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the infection is clearing up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and your breathing should keep improving. We’ll keep you on IV cefepime for a few more days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I switch to oral antibiotics later?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, infectious disease recommends 14 days total. You’ll switch to ciprofloxacin pills before discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs today show your white count is still high, but that’s expected with inflammation from your condition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that normal for me? I remember it was high last time too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your history of relapsing polychondritis and ___ syndrome can keep your WBC elevated even without infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the NTM my last culture showed? Is that being treated?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Infectious disease decided not to treat it now. It’s unclear if it’s active, and we didn’t want to add more antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your second bronchoscopy went well. We dilated again and took another biopsy. No new issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do they think the narrowing is getting worse over time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It seems the intervals between dilations are shortening, which suggests progression. But your rheumatology team is monitoring that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. What about my humidifier? You mentioned something about replacing it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, because Pseudomonas can live in equipment, we arranged for a new one. Please discard the old humidifier.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And I’ll keep using the tobramycin nebulizer at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, twice daily. It helps target Pseudomonas directly in your airways.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’re planning to discharge you today. You’re breathing comfortably on room air.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What meds will I be on at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue ciprofloxacin twice daily for one more week, tobramycin nebs twice daily, and the prednisone taper.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the taper is 20 mg, then 15, then 10, then back to 7.5 mg?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’ll give you clear instructions. Also, follow up with pulmonary and infectious disease soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if I start feeling worse again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call your doctor or come back if you have fever, increased shortness of breath, or more secretions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, Dr. Lee. I feel much better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’re glad to see your improvement. The team will get your discharge papers ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—should I avoid sick people?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, especially with your tracheostomy and immune suppression from prednisone. Try to stay away from crowds and sick contacts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. I’ll be careful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Also, keep using your albuterol as needed for tightness, and the guaifenesin to help thin mucus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Thanks again for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. We’re here to help. You’ll go home with your new humidifier and all your meds sorted.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. I’m ready to get back home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll have the discharge team finalize everything. Rest up, and take care.

summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___ was admitted for progressive dyspnea and increased sputum production in the setting of tracheostomy and recurrent tracheobronchial stenosis. He was found to have tracheobronchitis due to Pseudomonas aeruginosa, confirmed by sputum and bronchial cultures. He was treated with IV cefepime, later transitioned to oral ciprofloxacin, and received two bronchoscopies with balloon dilation of the trachea and left main bronchus. His prednisone dose was increased to 20 mg daily to reduce airway inflammation and then tapered. A new humidifier was arranged due to risk of equipment contamination. He improved clinically, maintained oxygenation on room air, and was discharged home with follow-up planned in pulmonary and infectious disease clinics.
